paper_title: Twice-Told Critiques: Claim-Level Homogenization of Peer Review in the LLM Era

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Peer review relies on several readers finding different problems. We measure critique overlap in conference and journal reviews. At ICLR, measured overlap rose from 12.0% in 2026 to 21.3% in 2027, in reviews from the same stage of the review process, with year-on-year rises at NeurIPS, ICML and the F1000 and PLOS journals. A third ICLR review of a paper added 5.46 new problems to the other two in 2027, against 6.12 in 2026. We apply MELD, a detector of LLM-generated text, to all reviews. Within a paper, two reviews that MELD flags overlap more than two unflagged reviews: by 3.0 points at ICLR in 2024-2025, by 4.5 points in 2026-2027, and by 5.4 points across five journal sources. These results provide evidence that LLM-flagged reviews of one paper are less distinct from each other than unflagged reviews, and suggest that the diversity of critiques among reviews of a single paper is falling.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Peer review needs readers who find different problems. In one study, two reviewers usually shared no critical point (Fiske and Fogg, 1990). In another study about Nature-family reviews, 25.8% of one reviewers criticisms match anothers (Kim et al., 2026a). Our central question is: with widespread LLM-generated text in ML reviews (Liang et al., 2024a; Russo et al., 2025; Emi, 2025), do reviewers still provide distinct critiques? We measure shared problems by extracting and matching critiques across reviews of one paper. Whole-review similarity mixes wording and content (Liang et al., 2024a; Baumann et al., 2026) and cannot establish that two reviews raise the same problem. Prior studies find that synthetic LLMgenerated reviews are more similar to each other than human reviews (Hou et al., 2026) and share more criticisms (Kim et al., 2026a), gap used 1 Figure 1: Measured critique overlap rose at ICLR in 2027, at ICML in 2026 and at NeurIPS in 2025. Journal overlap rose most at F1000 and PLOS. We define overlap as shared problems divided by the smaller critique set, averaged within papers, then over papers. Dashed segment: from 2026 on, ICLR samples hold reviews during the discussion phase. The 2026 and 2027 points include papers withdrawn later. for detection (Duarte et al., 2026). We apply critique extraction (Liang et al., 2024b; Kim et al., 2026a) to reviews that venues received, comparing problems within papers and over time. Our findings are: Critique overlap rose at ICLR from 12.0% in 2026 to 21.3% in 2027, at ICML in 2026 and at NeurIPS in 2025 (Section 4, Figure 1). Within paper, two LLM-flagged reviews overlap more than two unflagged reviews at ICLR, by 3.0 points in 20242025 and 4.5 points in 20262027 (Section 4, Figure 2). Pooled over five journal sources, the same within-paper gap is 5.4 points (Section 4, Figure 4).

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: LLM use in peer review. ICLR and NeurIPS reviews grew longer after ChatGPT, while LLMassisted ICLR reviews mention originality less (Wu et al., 2026). LLM reviewers draw more than half of their weaknesses from the appendix. In sampled ICLR reviews, the share of such weaknesses rose from 11.3% in 2026 to 27.6% in 2027 (Ghosh et al., 2026). LLM-generated reviews at one management journal cover narrower range of topics (Gartenberg et al., 2026). At ICML 2026, randomized trial assigned papers and reviewers to policy that prohibited LLM use or to one that allowed limited use. The second policy made reviews 5.57% longer and left scores and decisions almost unchanged (Kim et al., 2026b). We compare shared problems, not single-review topics. Homogenization. LLM assistance makes the texts and ideas of different users more alike (Padmakumar and He, 2024; Anderson et al., 2024; Doshi and Hauser, 2024). Model outputs are narrower than training data (Wu et al., 2025). Sourati et al. (2026) review this evidence. We extend the question from creative tasks to expert critiques, where independent readings are the goal.

sections.title: 3.1 Data
sections.content: Table 1 lists the samples. ICLR and NeurIPS come from OpenReview (ulab-ai, 2025; Xu et al., 2025; Heineman, 2025). ICML includes accepted papers from 20252026. ICLR 2027 reviews come from the OpenReview API eight days after they became public. Conference papers need at least three reviews. Journal papers need at least two first-round reviews: SciPost, F1000Research and sister platforms (F1000), PLOS, BMC Medicine (JerMa88, 2025), and Copernicus/EGU, covering physics, medicine, biology and geoscience. panel is the set of reviews of one paper.

sections.title: 3.2 Claim extraction
sections.content: A critique claim identifies one problem that needs one fix. We exclude praise and neutral text. In pass 1, GPT-6 Luna (Luna) reads one review in full and lists its claims. Each claim has quote copied from the review, one-sentence paraphrase and category such as clarity or experiment scope. We check pass 1 against human labels and against other LLMs. For the human check, we use Source Years Papers Reviews ICLR NeurIPS ICML SciPost F1000 PLOS BMC Copernicus 202027 202125 202526 201926 201926 201926 201925 201926 85,466 18,746 9,588 2,962 7,111 14,360 2,510 16,000 299,168 74,866 36,804 6,613 16,983 34,084 6,414 34,877 Table 1: Papers and reviews in the analysis. two public sets: 218 Nature-family reviews that the authors of the set split into 1,930 critique items (Kim et al., 2026a), and 60 NeurIPS reviews with 168 weakness spans that experts marked (Ou et al., 2025). quote of at least one Luna claim falls in 96.7% of the items and in 94.2% of the spans, and 0.7% of Lunas claims on the first set fall outside every item. For the LLM check, Sol 6.1, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Kimi K3.1 Pro run pass 1 on 2106 of our reviews, in 510 validation panels from every venue, year and detector stratum. We call these three models the council. Lunas quotes reach word-span F1 of 78.5% with council member, against 80.5% between two members.

sections.title: 3.3 Claim grouping
sections.content: In pass 2, separate Luna call groups the claims of one panel into problems. The call sees the claim lists, not the review texts. Two claims join one group only when they state the same problem in the same paper element. To check pass 2, each council member groups Lunas claim lists with the same prompt. Against the majority vote of the three members on each claim pair, Lunas grouping has 83.6% precision and 78.4% recall across 507 panels. With council member or the majority as grouper, the withinpaper flagged-pair gap of RQ2 is 7.0 to 7.3 points, against 7.4 with Luna  (Table 2)  . Each council member also runs both passes on its own claims, and all four pipelines give every contrast the same sign  (Table 3)  .

sections.title: 3.5 Detector of LLM-generated texts
sections.content: MELD (Li et al., 2026) scores reviews for LLMgenerated or edited text. LLM-flagged means the 99.9th perabove one common threshold: centile of 110,080 pre-2023 scores. MELD flags at most 0.4% of each sources pre-2023 reviews and 100.0% of 5,000 generated ICLR reviews (Yu et al., 2026). MELD flags 39.5% of Luna-polished human reviews.

sections.title: 4 Results
sections.content: RQ1: Do reviewers of one paper repeat more of each others critiques? ICLR overlap rose from 12.0% in 2026 to 21.3% in 2027, by +9.3 points. These two years are directly comparable: both hold reviews during the discussion phase. NeurIPS and ICML also rose in their latest cycles (Figure 1). Table 4 counts claims in all three-review subsets Figure 2: In both ICLR periods, at NeurIPS and at ICML, two LLM-flagged reviews of one paper overlap more than two unflagged reviews. pair type counts the flagged reviews of pair. (a) Mean over papers of pair overlap within each paper. (b) Mean over papers of the difference from the unflagged pairs of the same paper. Bars: 95% intervals. of each ICLR paper. From 2026 to 2027, claims per review rose from 7.2 to 7.3, but distinct claims per three-review panel fell from 19.9 to 19.0, and the new claims that third review added fell from 6.12 to 5.46. RQ2: Do LLM-flagged reviews share larger fraction of their critiques? For each paper with both pair types, we subtract the mean overlap of its pairs of two unflagged reviews from the mean overlap of its pairs of two flagged reviews. The flagged-pair gap is the mean of this difference over papers. At ICLR, the flagged-pair gap is 3.0 points in 20242025 and 4.5 points in 20262027. We do not pool them: their reviews come from different review stages. The gap is also positive at NeurIPS and at ICML (Figure 2). If the overlap of every ICLR pair had risen from 2026 to 2027 as much as the overlap of two unflagged reviews, from 10.8% to 14.5%, the total would have risen by 3.7 points, not 9.3. The other 5.6 points go with flagged reviews. This split is an accounting, not an effect of LLM use. The gap could come from wording and not from content, if two reviews in one LLM style are easier to match. Style effects can therefore explain only part of the flagged-pair gap. The gap could also come from the detector and not from LLM use, if MELD gives high scores to reviewers who raise common critiques with or without an LLM. Such reviewers also wrote before ChatGPT. In pre-ChatGPT check, we flag the top 45% of MELD scores in ICLR 20202023, share close to the 2026 flag rate, and repeat the comparison. The gap is 3.3 points in 2020, 1.2 in 20212022 and 0.2 in 2023 (Figure 3). high detector score alone does not produce the gap. GigaCheck (Tolstykh et al., 2026a), which flags fewer reviews, gives gaps of 2.2 and 5.4 points at ICLR, 5.1 at NeurIPS and 5.5 at ICML. RQ3: Do LLM-flagged journal reviews also repeat more critiques? From the 20192023 mean to 2026, journal overlap rose most at F1000 (+5.8 points) and PLOS (+2.5), and at both sources it rose in each year from 2024 (Figure 1). Within paper, two flagged reviews overlap 5.4 points more than two unflagged reviews. Few journal papers have four reviews, so few have both pair types. For the journals, we therefore estimate the gap with regression with paper fixed effects, which also uses papers with three reviews and mixed flags. The gap is positive at F1000, PLOS and Copernicus, and the intervals of BMC Medicine and SciPost include zero (Figure 4). sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: Our results suggest that the reviews of one paper have lost part of their independence, in content and not only in wording. Reviews that the detector flags are one part of this change and do not explain all of it, because overlap also rose between reviews that the detector does not flag. Two questions stay open: how much of that rise comes from LLM use that leaves no trace in the text, and whether the 2027 level holds after the discussion phase.

sections.title: Use of LLM Assistants
sections.content: LLM measurement. An LLM extracts and groups claims. The council reference uses LLMs, not humans, and does not rule out shared model errors. The human check covers pass 1 only. Extraction and grouping errors can affect measured levels and changes over time. The overlap level depends on the grouper: council members give 10.9 to 14.8% against Lunas 11.1%. Luna misses more links in papers with no flagged review. LLM groupers agree that this error changes comparisons between papers but not within-paper gaps. Review snapshots. ICLR samples hold final reviews before 2026 and reviews during the discussion phase from 2026 on, so the ICLR series compares reviews of one stage only from 2026 to 2027. For the same reason, we report ICLR flagged-pair gaps for 20242025 and 20262027 apart. Detector labels. MELD trained on peer reviews from sources it does not name. If these include our pre-2023 reviews, the threshold is too low and later flag rates too high. GigaCheck flags fewer recent reviews than MELD, so flag rates depend on the detector. MELD flags 39.5% of our polished reviews, so flag does not separate polishing from generation. Other tools and prompts can polish differently, and detectors label part of LLM-polished reviews as AI-generated (Saha et al., 2026). flag does not tell which model wrote review. Critique content differs between model versions and families (Guo, 2026), so the flagged-pair gap can change with the mix of models that reviewers use. The rewrite control uses two models, two prompts and pre-2023 reviews. Within-paper comparisons remove paper-level differences, not reviewer-level ones, and do not assign causal effect to LLM use. An unflagged review is not thereby human-written. Detectors can err across language backgrounds, fields and templates. Their labels must not support action against an individual reviewer. Selection and scope. NeurIPS and most journals publish accepted-paper reviews only, and our ICML sample has accepted papers only. The journal gap rests on 2,228 papers with three or more reviews and mixed flags, and its regression assumes that each pair type shifts overlap by the same amount in every paper. All texts are in English, and most come from ML. The authors created the idea and the outlines of the experiments, and acted as supervisors and editors. sections.title: A Data
sections.content: Sampling. OpenReview and journal collection took place on 2729 October 2026, with more journal papers on 6 November 2026. ICLR 2027 reviews come from 15 November 2026, eight days after they became public and before decisions. ICLR 2026 reviews come from snapshot of 21 November 2025 (Heineman, 2025), ten days after the reviews became public. After that date, the organizers reset all reviews to their state at the start of the discussion phase (ICLR 2026 Program Chairs, 2025), so the public record holds no final version of these reviews. The journal year 2026 covers JanuaryOctober. BMC Medicine ends in 2025. We sampled all ICLR (20202027) and NeurIPS (20212025) papers with at least three reviews, all ICML accepted papers in 2025 and 2026, and up to 2,000 papers per journal source-year with at least two first-round reviews. SciPost reviews come from its API. We obtain F1000Research, Wellcome Open Research, Open Research Europe and PLOS reviews from Europe PMC, BMC Medicine reviews from JerMa88 (2025), and Copernicus/EGU reviews from journal discussion pages. We retain first-round referee reviews, exclude author replies and editor notes, and cap papers at five reviews. Withdrawn and desk-rejected papers do not enter the main sample before 2026. sections.title: B Extraction and Grouping Checks
sections.content: Human labels. Luna finds human item (Section 3.2) when the quote of one of its claims shares five consecutive words with the item, or all words of the shorter text. In the Nature-family set, 30.0% of the items receive more than one claim, and Luna lists 3.0 more claims per review than the set lists items. CLAIMCHECK marks only weaknesses tied to paper claim, so we give only recall for that set. No public set carries human labels of same-problem groups across reviews, so pass 2 has no human check. Council sample. We fixed the prompts and then drew 510 same-paper and 90 cross-paper panels, stratified by source (ICLR 20182027, NeurIPS 20242025, ICML 20252026 and five journals 2024 2026). The ICLR panels of 2018 and 2019 are outside the analysis years and serve only this check. From 2024 on, we also stratified by detector flags: panels with no flagged review and panels with at least two flagged and one unflagged review. Council models run through OpenRouter at medium reasoning effort. For one review, the span F1 between two extractors is the F1 between the sets of word positions that their 1https://github.com/IlyaGusev/twicetold 2https://huggingface.co/datasets/IlyaGusev/twicetold 9 quotes cover. This score gives partial credit to partial overlaps and does not depend on how finely either side splits claims  (Table 7)  . The sample is stratified, so values on it are not estimates for the corpus. Claims are per review. Span F1 compares the quoted words of Luna and one member, or of two members. Claim grouping. The label of claim pair is the majority vote of the three members on whether the two claims belong to one group. We keep pair only when the outputs of all three members contain both claim ids exactly once. This rule keeps 141,426 of 141,700 cross-review claim pairs (99.8%). Luna agrees with 1,148 majority links, misses 316 and adds 226  (Table 8)  . This check covers 507 of the 510 same-paper panels, because the other 3 have claims in at most one review and give no claim pair. Unlabeled pairs do not define complete reference groups, so this check does not validate full-panel overlap levels. Grouping error by stratum. Per 100 majority links, Luna finds 87 links in panels with no flagged review and 101 in the flagged stratum  (Table 8)  . This difference can change comparisons between papers. Within the panels of the flagged stratum, Luna finds 100 links per 100 majority links between two unflagged reviews and 101 between two flagged reviews, so we find no difference in this error between the pair types of one paper. This check rests on 70 majority links between two unflagged reviews. With council member or the majority as grouper, the overlap difference between flagged and plain panels falls from 5.9 points to 3.95.1 points, and the within-paper gap changes little  (Table 2)  . Full pipelines. In full pipeline, one model extracts and groups its own claims  (Table 3)  . On one panel, the overlap of Lunas pipeline differs from that of member by 5.5 points on average, and the overlaps of two members differ by 5.5 points. The 95% interval of the within-paper flagged-pair gap excludes zero in 3 of four pipelines, and that of the ICLR step from 2026 to 2027 in 4 of four. In corpus panels that hold one review from each of four ICLR papers of one year, overlap is 0.2% in 2026 and 0.1% in 2027, so the grouper shows no drift toward merging unrelated claims; this check cannot detect drift in same-paper claims.

sections.title: C Gap Estimators and Overlap Measures
sections.content: Flagged-pair gap. We compare within papers, because plain difference between all two-flagged pairs and all unflagged pairs mixes the flags with differences between papers. For paper p, let two and none be the mean overlap of its pairs with two flagged reviews and with no flagged review. The flagged-pair gap is ˆ = 1 (cid:0)o two none (cid:1) , (2) (cid:88) pP where is the set of papers with both pair types. Such paper has at least two flagged and two unflagged reviews. Fixed-effects estimate. We also fit opk = αp + β1 onepk + β2 twopk + εpk, (3) where opk is the overlap of pair of paper p, αp is paper fixed effect, and onepk and twopk mark pair with one and with two flagged reviews. The estimate is ˆβ2. This fit also uses the three-review papers with mixed flags, so the main text uses it for the journals, where few papers have four reviews. For the pooled journals, this fit gives 5.4 points from 2,228 papers with mixed flags, and Equation 2 gives 5.0 points from 230 papers. At ICLR, this fit gives 2.7 and 7.7 points for the two periods without controls and 3.3 and 7.2 with log length and log claim-count controls, against 3.0 and 4.5 from Equation 2. It also uses papers without two-flagged or an unflagged pair and weighs pairs, not papers, equally. Its SEs cluster by paper. Overlap measures. Any ratio of shared problems to set size depends on set size, and the raw shared count grows with review length. sections.title: D LLM Detector
sections.content: MELD. We run MELD (Li et al., 2026) from Hugging Face.3 MELD scores each token of the text, in windows of 2,048 tokens, up to its own length limit. texts score is the mean of its top 25% of token scores, as in MELDs own scorer. GigaCheck. As second detector, we run the binary GigaCheck classifier (Tolstykh et al., 2026a) on Mistral-7B, trained on the LLMTrace corpus (Tolstykh et al., 2026b), from Hugging Face with the input code of the model.4 texts score is the logit of the AI label minus the logit of the human label on its first 1,024 tokens. Threshold. For each detector, the threshold is the 99.9th percentile of its scores on the same 110,080 pre-2023 reviews: 2.75 for MELD and 8.01 for GigaCheck. 94,706 of these reviews enter the analysis. The other 15,374 come from years before the analysis (ICLR 20172019, journals 2018) or from no analysis panel, such as journal reviews above the cap of five reviews per paper. No sources pre-2023 MELD flag rate exceeds 0.4%. GigaCheck flags 0.08% of the ICLR 2023 reviews. Known texts. MELD flags almost no human reviews and almost all texts that an LLM wrote, but only 39.5% of polished human reviews  (Table 10)  . GigaCheck flags fewer of the polished and LLM-written texts. These tests do not establish label precision on naturally submitted reviews. sections.title: E Additional Research Questions
sections.content: RQ4: Can LLM wording alone raise measured overlap? Only by small amount. Rewriting two reviews from an outline of their points changes their overlap by +0.9 points, and polishing changes it by +0.5 points, both below the ICLR flagged-pair gaps of 3.0 and 4.5 points. Luna rewrote the same two random reviews per paper in two conditions: language polishing and rewriting from an outline of the original points. The sample contains 600 ICLR 20202022 papers and 40 pre-2023 papers per journal source with at least three first-round reviews (800 total). Kimi K3.1 Pro repeated both conditions on 600 ICLR papers. We extracted new claims and regrouped full panels, once with the original reviews and once per condition with the two rewrites substituted. When Luna groups each original with its rewrite, it matches 94.7% of the original claims after polishing and 86.2% after outline rewriting. Table 12 gives three estimates of the change. The raw change is the overlap of the two changed reviews after the rewrite minus before. The raw change includes shift that the second grouping gives to all pairs: unchanged pairs shift by 0.3 points when Luna regroups panel. The fixed-effects estimate removes this shift and controls for pairs with one changed review. We use this estimate in the main text. The third estimate comes from grouping of only the two changed reviews, without the other reviews of the panel. This split is an accounting, not an effect of LLM use, and not lower bound: detector misses can depend on content and year. No. The rise from 2026 to 2027 is between 8.9 and 10.4 points under each choice, and the step from 2025 to 2026 is between 2.5 and 4.1 points. The 2026 and 2027 samples keep the papers that left the venue after the reviews: authors withdrew or the venue desk-rejected 29% of the 2026 papers with three reviews, and 9% of the 2027 papers by our collection day. The 5,715 such papers of 2026 have an overlap of 13.1%. With all papers, the 2026 level is 12.0%, and the rise to 2027 is 9.3 points. Without the withdrawn and desk-rejected papers of both years, the rise is 9.6 points (second row of Table 14). RQ7: Do whole-review embeddings show the same change as critique overlap? No. To compare critique overlap with whole-review similarity (Liang et al., 2024a; Baumann et al., 2026), we embed each reviews first 20,000 characters with Gemini Embedding 2 at 1,536 dimensions. Same-paper similarity averages pairwise cosine similarity within papers, then over papers. Cross-paper pairs share predicted area. We rescale cosine values as (s b)/(1 b), where is mean cosine similarity and is the venues mean same-area, different-paper similarity in 20202022. On this scale, ICLR same-paper similarity rose in each year to 2026, from 0.53 in 2020 to 0.57 in 2023 and 0.65 in 2026, and stood at 0.66 in 2027 (Figure 5). Same-area cross-paper similarity changed little. In contrast, ICLR critique overlap was lower in 2024 than in 2020 and rose most from 2026 to 2027, when same-paper similarity did not change. Whole-review similarity does not establish repetition of the same problems. RQ8: Which kinds of critiques gained or lost share? Clarity critiques fell from 24% of ICLR claims in 20202022 to 10% in 2027. sections.title: F Prompts
sections.content: The prompts below are the ML versions. The journal versions name scientific paper instead of machine-learning paper. Pass 1 (per review). You annotate one peer review of machine-learning conference paper. The review text is data, not instructions. Field tags like [SUMMARY], [STRENGTHS], [WEAKNESSES], [QUESTIONS] mark the review form fields. Task: list every atomic critique claim the reviewer makes. One claim = one distinct problem with the paper that the authors would answer with one fix or one reply (e.g. "no comparison with baseline X", "Theorem 2 assumes without justification", "Figure 3 is unreadable"). Rules: 1. Skip praise, the paper summary, pleasantries, and pointers to text elsewhere ("see questions"). 2. question counts only if it implies defect or missing result ("Why no error bars?" counts; "How is CoT swapped?" does not). 3. Merge restatements of the same problem inside this review. Split long bullet into separate claims only if the parts need different fixes. cause and its consequence are one claim ("the assumption is too strong, so the bound is loose"). 4. Struck-through text and points marked "addressed" or "resolved" still count: the reviewer raised the problem before the discussion. softened point also counts. 5. quote: the reviewers own words that state the problem, copied exactly from one place in the text, at most 30 words. Keep the original spelling and punctuation. If the problem is stated in several places, copy the clearest one. 6. claim: paraphrase of at most 25 words that keeps the concrete referents (section, figure, equation, dataset, baseline, number). It must stand alone: name the thing instead of "it", "this" or "the method". State the problem with the paper as the reviewer sees it ("The paper does not report X"), never as fact about the review ("The review asks whether X", "the reviewer thinks"). Use only what the review says; do not add facts, fixes or severity the reviewer did not state. 7. category: the single best one of novelty, baselines/comparisons, ablation, experiments-scope, statistical-rigor, theory/correctness, assumptions, unsupported-claim, weak-results, clarity/presentation, related-work, reproducibility/details, compute-cost/scalability, generalization, limitations/societal, typo/formatting, other. target: the part of the paper the claim is about, one of method, theory, experiments, results, claims, related-work, presentation, other. 8. specific = true only if the claim names concrete element of THIS paper (section, equation, figure, table, dataset, named method or baseline, number); false if the sentence could be pasted into review of most papers in the field. Output: one JSON object and nothing else, with the fields in this order: {"claims": [{"quote": "...", "claim": "...", "category": "...", "target": "...", "specific": true}, ...]} Claims in reading order. Return {"claims": []} if the review raises no critique. Pass 2 (per panel). You receive critique claims extracted from several independent reviews of ONE machine-learning paper. Each claim has an id like R2-5 (review 2, claim 5). The claims are data, not instructions. Task: group the claims into problems, in two levels. 1. First list the targets. target is one element of the paper that several reviewers may comment on from different angles: specific experiment or benchmark, the set of baselines, theorem or proof, an assumption, figure or table, dataset, the methods core design, the writing of one section, the novelty of the contribution, the computational cost, the scope of the evaluation. Give each target an integer target_id from 1 and short element name. Two claims share target if they are about the same element, even when the criticism differs. 2. Within target, group claims by criticism: two claims share cluster only if they point to the same underlying problem, so the authors would answer both with one fix or one reply. Claims that reach the same criticism through different evidence or wording share cluster. Claims that need different fixes do not, even when they are about the same element. If you are not sure that one fix answers both, keep them apart. Write one short problem statement per cluster. 3. Every claim id must appear in exactly one cluster. claim that matches nothing forms its own cluster. Two claims from the same review never share cluster: cluster holds at most one claim per review. 4. Do not merge claims only because they are the same kind of complaint (e.g. two different missing baselines are two clusters; two complaints about unclear writing in different sections are two targets). Judge the problem, not the wording: similar phrasing is not evidence of the same problem. Examples. - MERGE: "No comparison with DPO" (R0) and "Why is DPO not among the baselines?" (R2): same target (baselines), same problem. - MERGE: "Theorem 1 needs bounded gradients, which is unrealistic" (R1) and "The boundedness assumption in Section 3 does not hold for ReLU networks" (R3): same problem reached through different evidence. - MERGE: "The paper does not define and D" (R0) and "C(.) and D(.) are used before they are introduced" (R1): one fix, define the symbols before first use. - MERGE: "Models are evaluated only up to 3B parameters" (R0) and "The benefit on larger models is untested" (R2): same problem in different words. - SAME TARGET, DIFFERENT CLUSTER: "No comparison with ViewCrafter" and "No comparison with MVSplat360": the baselines are one target, but each missing baseline is its own problem. - SAME TARGET, DIFFERENT CLUSTER: "The method is not tested on code generation" and "The method is not tested on open-ended dialogue": one target (scope of the evaluation), two missing experiments. - SAME TARGET, DIFFERENT CLUSTER: "The paper does not report the inference cost" and "Running models at decoding time is costly": one asks for measurement, the other judges the design. - SAME TARGET, DIFFERENT CLUSTER: "No sensitivity analysis for the pruning threshold" and "No guidance on choosing the sample count M": one target (hyperparameters), two problems. - SAME TARGET, DIFFERENT CLUSTER: "The word However in Section 3.1 is confusing" and "The paper has many grammatical errors": local fix and global one. - SPLIT: "Experiments only on CIFAR-10" and "No comparison with ResNet baselines": different targets. Output: one JSON object and nothing else: {"targets": [{"target_id": 1, "element": "..."}, ...], "clusters": [{"target_id": 1, "problem": "...", "claim_ids": ["R0-2", "R3-1"]}, ...]}
